#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)
Description: The Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) is normally a triennial cross-sectional survey of U.S. families. The survey data include information on families’ balance sheets, pensions, income, and demographic characteristics. Information is also included from related surveys of pension providers and the earlier such surveys conducted by the Federal Reserve Board. No other study for the country collects comparable information. Data from the SCF are widely used, from analysis at the Federal Reserve and other branches of government to scholarly work at the major economic research centers.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)
Description: The Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) is normally a triennial cross-sectional survey of U.S. families. The survey data include information on families’ balance sheets, pensions, income, and demographic characteristics. Information is also included from related surveys of pension providers and the earlier such surveys conducted by the Federal Reserve Board. No other study for the country collects comparable information. Data from the SCF are widely used, from analysis at the Federal Reserve and other branches of government to scholarly work at the major economic research centers.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Report: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)

## 1. Checking your description

**Your description is accurate.** It matches the official text on the Federal Reserve Board's "About the SCF" page and its Data.gov catalog entry almost word for word. The official version continues with three more facts you may want to add:

> "The survey has contained a panel element over two periods. Respondents to the 1983 survey were re-interviewed in 1986 and 1989. Respondents to the 2007 survey were re-interviewed in 2009. The study is sponsored by the Federal Reserve Board in cooperation with the Department of the Treasury. Since 1992, data have been collected by NORC at the University of Chicago."

Three points to keep in mind:
- **"Normally triennial."** The Fed says it has run the modern survey every three years since 1989. The earlier years (1983, plus re-interviews in 1986 and 2009) were irregular, which is why the text says "normally."
- **"Families"** has a specific technical meaning, the "primary economic unit." It is not the Census Bureau's household or family definition (see §6).
- **"No other study for the country collects comparable information."** The Fed's paperwork filings with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) make the same claim, calling the SCF "the only source of representative information on the structure of U.S. families' finances."

## 2. Key facts

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Publisher | Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Division of Research and Statistics |
| Partner | U.S. Department of the Treasury; the IRS Statistics of Income Division (SOI) supplies the wealthy-household sample |
| Data collector | NORC at the University of Chicago (since 1992); earlier, the University of Michigan's Survey Research Center |
| Form number / OMB control no. | FR 3059 / OMB 7100-0287 (current approval expires Aug. 31, 2027) |
| Frequency | Every three years |
| Unit | U.S. "families" (primary economic units); 131.3 million households represented in 2022 |
| Latest released survey | 2022 (released Oct. 18, 2023): 4,602 interviews (3,298 from the area sample, 1,304 from the list sample) |
| Survey in progress | 2025: up to 7,000 interviews, about 110 minutes each, fielded roughly March/April 2025 to early 2026 |
| Main portal | https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm |
| Catalogs | Data.gov ("survey-of-consumer-finances-scf"); the Fed's own data catalog |
| Cost to users | Free public download |

**Is the 2025 data out?** I found no published 2025 results. The OMB paperwork said "very preliminary results" would reach the Board in mid-2026. Going by past schedules (the 2022 data came out in October 2023), public release would be around late 2026. Check the SCF index page for the current status.

## 3. Who publishes it and how it's made

- **Federal Reserve Board.** Staff design the questionnaire, draw the sample of wealthy households, process and impute the data, protect respondent privacy, publish the data, and write the flagship report in the *Federal Reserve Bulletin*.
- **NORC.** Builds the general random sample of addresses, recruits respondents, and conducts interviews by tablet (in person, by phone, or by Zoom). Interviewers carry NORC photo ID, and respondents can call 1-800-609-2911 to verify.
- **IRS Statistics of Income Division.** Under a contract, SOI provides statistical records derived from tax returns. These are used to oversample wealthy households. The arrangement is built so that:
  - the Board never receives respondents' names,
  - SOI never receives data linking survey answers to tax records, and
  - NORC never receives the tax-derived income data.
- **Funding.** The Fed funds the survey itself, not through congressional appropriations. That makes it less exposed to budget fights than many statistical programs. On the other hand, the survey is discretionary (see §4).

## 4. Legal authority

- **Statutory basis.** The Fed's Federal Register notices cite two sections of the Federal Reserve Act:
  - **Section 2A (12 U.S.C. 225a):** the Board and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) must promote maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.
  - **Section 12A (12 U.S.C. 263):** the FOMC conducts open market operations with regard to "the general credit situation of the country."
  
  The Board says it uses SCF data to help meet these obligations.
- **No specific mandate.** No law requires an SCF by name. It rests on the Fed's general authority, so it could in principle be cut back or ended by Board decision. That matters for preservation planning.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act.** The survey is approved by OMB as collection FR 3059. The Board renews it under authority delegated by OMB, with public notices in the Federal Register (most recently 89 FR 61423, July 31, 2024, extended without revision). An earlier renewal cycle (2021) received no public comments.
- **Voluntary.** No one is required to respond.
- **Confidentiality.** Information that identifies individuals may be withheld from Freedom of Information Act requests under the personal-privacy exemption (5 U.S.C. 552(b)(6)). Tax-derived sample information is governed by IRS confidentiality rules. Pretest data are never released.

## 5. History

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1946 | The Fed sponsored its first consumer finance survey, conducted by the USDA Bureau of Agricultural Economics, to understand the liquid assets households built up during World War II and their pent-up spending. |
| 1947–1970 | The University of Michigan's Survey Research Center ran annual "Surveys of Consumer Finances" (led by George Katona), focused on purchase plans, credit, and liquid assets. These are archived at ICPSR (Series 55). |
| 1962–63 | The Fed's one-time Survey of Financial Characteristics of Consumers (with the 1963 Survey of Changes in Family Finances) was the first detailed wealth survey. It pioneered the two-part sample design, with Census Bureau interviewers. A 1965 follow-up was lost because there was never money to keypunch the paper questionnaires. |
| 1977 | Survey of Consumer Credit, sponsored by the federal banking agencies, a direct ancestor of the modern credit questions. |
| 1983 | **The modern SCF begins.** Sponsors were the Fed, the Department of Health and Human Services (which wanted pension data and supplied most of the funding), and five other agencies. Interviews: 3,824. An IRS-based wealthy sample was used under tight limits. Key people: Robert Avery (director), Glenn Canner, Barbara Lowery, Fritz Scheuren (SOI), Thomas Gustafson (HHS), Richard Curtin (Michigan). |
| 1983 / 1989 | Related surveys of pension providers collected plan details from respondents' employers. These are the "surveys of pension providers" your description mentions. |
| 1986, 1989 | Re-interviews of the 1983 panel (the 1983–89 Panel SCF). |
| 1989 | The current sample design and triennial schedule settle in. This is the usual starting point for comparable time series. |
| 1992 | NORC becomes the data collector. |
| 2007–2009 | Special re-interview in 2009 of 2007 respondents to measure the effects of the Great Recession. |
| 2019 | The Distributional Financial Accounts launch: quarterly wealth-distribution estimates from 1989 onward, built on the SCF. |
| 2022 | The general sample is redesigned to oversample certain racial and ethnic groups. Interviews become possible by phone or video. Median net worth rose 37% over 2019, the largest three-year gain in the modern survey. |
| 2025 | Fieldwork for the newest survey, with a cap of up to 7,000 interviews. |

## 6. Content and methods (for data scientists)

**Content.** Assets of every kind (bank and brokerage accounts, stocks, bonds, mutual funds, retirement accounts, pensions, homes, other real estate, vehicles, privately held businesses), debts (mortgages, home equity lines, credit cards, student and auto loans), income, work history, pension rights, use of financial institutions, inheritances, attitudes toward credit and risk, financial literacy, and demographics.

**Sample design.** Two parts, combined with weights:
1. A standard area sample (random addresses) for widely held items such as homeownership.
2. A "list sample" drawn from tax-derived records to oversample wealthy families, who hold most of the thinly held assets such as private businesses and tax-exempt bonds.

People on the **Forbes 400** list are excluded by design.

**Response rates (2022).** About 40%+ in the area sample, about one-third in the list sample, and about half that level among the wealthiest list strata.

**Missing data.** Imputed five times. The public file therefore has five "implicates" per family: 4,602 families become 23,010 records. Seven families were dropped to protect privacy, leaving **22,975 public records for 4,595 families**. Treating the rows as independent observations will make standard errors wrong; the Fed's download page warns about this explicitly.

**Variance estimation.** Users get bootstrap replicate weights (file X42001) plus SAS and Stata programs for standard errors that account for both the imputation and the sample design. Details of the sample design are not released.

**Privacy protections in the public file.** Some values are rounded or altered, detailed geography is withheld (the survey is reliable only at the national level), and some categories, including detailed race, are collapsed. See the codebook for specifics.

**Unit of analysis.** The "primary economic unit": the economically dominant individual or couple plus everyone financially interdependent with them. The survey uses its own conventions for choosing a "reference person." Read the codebook before comparing results with Census data.

**Files available for each survey:**
- Full public dataset (about 5,300 variables) in SAS (two transport formats), Stata (you need Stata SE to load every variable), and ASCII with a variable map.
- Summary extract: the variables used in the Fed's report, inflation-adjusted, in SAS, Stata, and CSV.
- The SDA online analysis tool, hosted by UC Berkeley.
- An interactive chartbook covering 1989–2022.
- Codebook, questionnaire outline, showcards, interview program source code, a "Changes for 2022" note, and a net-worth flowchart.

**Revisions.** Earlier survey years are periodically reprocessed (weights, error fixes, definitions). Numbers in new reports can differ from older ones, and files are updated after release; the 2022 summary extract was updated on April 3, 2024. Always record download dates.

## 7. Typical users

- **Federal Reserve:** FOMC and staff analysis, the Financial Stability Report, research papers and notes, and the quarterly Distributional Financial Accounts. When the SCF data come out, the DFA history is revised; the October 2023 release, for example, substantially raised estimates of younger Americans' wealth.
- **Other parts of government:** Treasury and IRS-SOI, the Congressional Budget Office (wealth-distribution reports), the Government Accountability Office, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Social Security Administration and the Department of Labor (retirement and pensions), and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (banking).
- **Academics:** wealth inequality, saving and portfolio choice, household debt, retirement security, the racial wealth gap, business ownership, and estimates of how much a wealth tax could raise.
- **Think tanks and advocates:** for example, the Urban Institute, Brookings, the Employee Benefit Research Institute, the Center for Retirement Research, and organizations focused on racial and economic justice.
- **Journalists and industry:** it is the standard source for "median net worth," "racial wealth gap," and "share with credit card debt" statistics. Financial firms use it for market sizing.

## 8. Benefits to the public

- **Unique measurement.** It is the only nationally representative source that captures the whole family balance sheet together with reliable coverage of the top of the wealth distribution.
- **A long time series.** Comparable data since 1989 (with roots in 1946) track inflation-adjusted net worth, homeownership, retirement readiness, and debt burdens. For example, in 2022 the median payment-to-income ratio for debtors hit a record-low 13.4%, and the homeownership rate was 66.1%.
- **Equity analysis.** Wealth gaps by race and ethnicity, age, education, and income, made more precise by the 2022 oversample.
- **Policy evaluation.** Tax policy, retirement policy, student debt, consumer credit rules, and responses to crises (the 2009 re-interview, pandemic-era changes).
- **Openness.** Free microdata, documentation, and code, with strong privacy safeguards that protect public trust.

## 9. Notes for preservationists and data librarians

- **What to capture for every year (1983–2022, plus 2025 when released):**
  - main data files in every format, the summary extract, and replicate weights;
  - codebook, interview program source, showcards, and "Changes" notes;
  - the SAS macro that defines the summary variables;
  - the *Bulletin* report (HTML and PDF), the chartbook, and historical tables.
- **Where things live:**
  - The Fed's "Previous Surveys" page covers 1962/63, 1983, 1986, 1983–89 panel, and later.
  - ICPSR Series 55 has the 1947–1970 Michigan surveys and the 1983 SCF.
  - The Data.gov harvest record carries the catalog description.
- **Version risk.** Silent updates to files and retroactive revisions mean you should record checksums and dates.
- **Policy-record risk.** Archive the OMB/Federal Register materials too: the FR 3059 notices and the Part A and B supporting statements (on reginfo.gov and omb.report). They document the survey's legal basis, sample design, and response rates.
- **Continuity risk.** The survey depends on Board discretion (no specific mandate), on the IRS-SOI agreement, and on a single contractor. Falling response rates among the wealthy are a known methodological pressure.
- **Rights.** The data are free to download. I did not find a formal license statement, so check the Fed's website terms for reuse and citation guidance.

## 10. Known limitations

- The Forbes 400 exclusion and low response at the very top mean the extreme tail is under-represented. The Fed's own research describes adjustments (for example, FEDS working paper 2021-053).
- There are no estimates below the national level, so it cannot be used for state or local analysis.
- Three-year gaps miss turning points; the Distributional Financial Accounts partly fill this.
- It is self-reported, so there is some error in values such as business and home worth.
- The data are mostly cross-sectional; the only panels are 1983–89 and 2007–09.
- Imputation and the complex sample design require specialized methods.
- Response rates have generally declined over time.
